For keeping a Wi-Fi router running during a power outage, the best power station is one with a large battery capacity (Wh) and low standby power consumption.

A typical Wi-Fi router consumes around 5–15 watts. That means a 1,000Wh power station could theoretically run it for 67–200 hours, although actual runtime will be lower because of conversion losses and the power station's own consumption.

One important detail: A larger power station doesn't always mean better efficiency. Some large stations consume 10–20W just keeping their AC inverter running, potentially using more electricity than the router itself.

For maximum runtime, powering the router directly from a compatible DC output is often much more efficient.

What matters is how much power the station consumes internally while supplying DC power, especially at low loads.

For example, if you're powering a 10W USB device:

A station consuming 2W internally loses about 17% of its total battery draw.

A station consuming 8W internally loses about 44%.

A station consuming 15W internally loses 60%.

That's why I would prioritize low DC idle consumption over battery capacity or inverter efficiency.

chats.answer:
If you're using only USB and 12V DC ports, the most efficient portable power station is not necessarily the one with the best advertised battery efficiency.

The key is to minimize three types of power loss:

Idle consumption: Power used by the station's electronics just to stay on.

DC conversion losses: Energy lost converting battery voltage to USB-C, USB-A, or regulated 12V.

Inverter standby losses: Some stations consume additional power when their AC inverter is enabled, even without an AC load.

For your use case, I would prioritize low DC idle consumption over inverter efficiency, especially if you're charging phones, running a router, or powering small 12V devices continuously.

chats.answer:
If you're using only USB and 12V DC ports, the most efficient portable power station is generally one that has:

Low DC idle consumption — ideally under 1–2 watts.

Efficient DC-to-DC converters — ideally 90–95% or better at your actual load.

No need to turn on the AC inverter — AC inverters can waste 5–20W or more just by being enabled.

Low overhead at small loads — particularly important if you're powering a phone, router, or 12V refrigerator for many hours.

The key distinction is that a power station can have excellent efficiency at 100W but poor efficiency at 5W.
